clue.text: Not quite right to speak in it?

definitions.text: Not quite right to speak in it?

parts.words: Not quite right to speak in it?
parts.note: a grammatical form named by words meaning 'not quite right', in which one speaks of unfinished past action

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether it is improper to talk in some setting.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'not quite right' as flawed and the thing you speak in as a verb form: the past continuous in grammar ('I was going') carries a name meaning faulty.
explanation.definitionFit: This grammatical aspect describes ongoing past action, and its first word also means flawed or less than right.

clue.text: One in France, it is one

parts.note: un is the French word for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a single thing in France is still a single thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit is a single item, the number one as a measure.

clue.text: Joint bent in submission

explanation.surface: A body part is flexed when someone yields.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the leg's hinge between thigh and shin, and kneeling down on it is the classic posture of yielding.

clue.text: Interrupt illegal act

explanation.surface: Someone cuts into a conversation, which is a crime.
explanation.definitionFit: To cut in on talk is one sense; the other is a burglary, forcing entry to a building.

clue.text: Gosh, a party was thrown for old mathematician

indicators.note: a party that is thrown is held, but here the letters are thrown about and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone exclaims that a celebration was held in honour of an ancient scholar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was thrown' rearranges GOSH, A and PARTY together into the Greek thinker's name.
explanation.definitionFit: He was the ancient Greek thinker behind the theorem on right-angled triangles.

clue.text: Muckraker makes something dirty last for a long time

parts.note: muds, wet earthy substances, are dirty stuff
to linger is to stay on or endure for a long time

explanation.surface: A scandal-digging journalist makes a mess that will not go away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes' is the link; the clue really reads as 'mud's linger', dirt that stays, with the S loosely supplied.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name someone who digs up or spreads scandal about others to damage them.

clue.text: Dull fellows of the cloth are unseen establishment figures

explanation.surface: Drab clergymen turn out to be the hidden powers of the state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of the cloth' suggests clergy, but here the cloth is simply the fabric of drab business wear.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally, chaps clad in drab tailoring; idiomatically, the anonymous officials who quietly wield power behind the scenes.

clue.text: Until the beer runs out?

parts.note: bitter is a British style of ale, so drinking until the last of it is gone is a phrase meaning to the very finish

explanation.surface: A drinker vows to stay at the pub until the supply is exhausted.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British style of beer; the idiom really means persisting to the very end however unpleasant.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means persisting right to the finish, and literally suggests drinking up the last drop of a pub ale.

clue.text: Stinging complaint?

parts.note: a stinging complaint sounds like a sharp grumble but is a skin ailment from a stinging weed

explanation.surface: Someone makes a sharp, cutting criticism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complaint' suggests a grievance, but it is a medical complaint: the itchy bumps from brushing a stinging weed.
explanation.definitionFit: Urticaria, the itchy rash raised by contact with a stinging plant, is literally a skin ailment caused by stings.

clue.text: Odd characters look up at diminutive lady!

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters, first, third and fifth, are picked from the words look up

explanation.surface: Strange people gaze upwards at a short woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd characters' looks like strange people, but it takes the first, third and fifth letters of 'look up'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a pet form of Louise or Louisa, so a shortened woman's name.

clue.text: Set about including a surfeit

indicators.note: including means the scrambled word takes a inside it
about signals that the letters of Set are moved around into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sets out to cover an excess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges SET to STE, and 'including' puts A inside it after the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to fill someone to excess, to glut with more than enough.

clue.text: A couple of pounds, that's as many as there are

indicators.note: a couple of means two copies of the abbreviation

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from the Latin libra

explanation.surface: A two-pound sum is presented as the full count of something.
explanation.walkthrough: L for pound comes from the Latin libra, as in the old £sd money.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means the whole number or every one, nothing left out.

clue.text: Disconcerting procrastination

explanation.surface: Delaying things is unsettling.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the words separately: putting things off, which is delay.
explanation.definitionFit: Unsettling or unpleasant is the usual sense; read as two words it describes putting things off, i.e. delaying.

clue.text: Awkward red-tape ie right to be included for secondary lodging

indicators.note: to be included means the letter for right goes inside the rearranged letters
awkward suggests the letters of red-tape and ie are jumbled into a clumsy new order

explanation.surface: Awkward bureaucracy is needed before you can include a second home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Awkward' rearranges RED-TAPE and IE; 'to be included' puts R (right) among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This French phrase names a small flat or house kept for occasional stays besides one's main home.

clue.text: Relaxed, what shoplifter did was not difficult, some might say

definitions.text: what shoplifter did was not difficult, some might say

explanation.surface: A thief found their stealing easy.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense reads the phrase loosely as 'stole it easily'; 'some might say' admits the grammar is stretched.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means rested or did not exert oneself; read literally it describes a thief stealing something easily.

clue.text: In Brazil, expected to find holly

indicators.note: In signals that the answer sits inside the run of letters Brazil, expected

explanation.surface: A traveller hopes to come across a certain shrub in South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' takes the letters straddling the end of 'Brazil' and the start of 'expected'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the botanical genus name of the evergreen with prickly leaves and red berries.

clue.text: Stepwise arrangement of hierarchy?

explanation.surface: Someone asks about the layered structure of an organisation.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a staggered formation of troops, ships or aircraft, and also a rank or level in an organisation's pecking order.

clue.text: Amphibian pecked aquatic plant

parts.note: a frog is an amphibian
bit means pecked, struck with the mouth

explanation.surface: A frog was nipped by a bird near a pond weed.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small floating pond weed with round leaves, found in still fresh water.

clue.text: Putting in the first three

explanation.surface: A golfer is putting their way into the top three.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting' suggests golf, but it means setting down; the second sense is a racing term.
explanation.definitionFit: Setting or positioning is the first sense; in horse racing, finishing first, second or third is a place.

clue.text: Tailless animal in portico

indicators.note: tailless means the final letter of the animal's name is cut off

parts.note: a stoat is a small animal of the weasel family

explanation.surface: An animal with no tail is found sheltering in a colonnade.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek architecture it is a covered walkway or colonnade, a roofed porch with pillars.

clue.text: Draw tail, result disastrous

indicators.note: a disastrous result is a wreck, so the letters of tail and result are smashed and rebuilt

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sketches a tail and the outcome is terrible.
explanation.definitionFit: To depict in pictures, to make drawings for a book, is the same as to draw.

clue.text: Make lace using inferior articles

explanation.surface: Someone makes lace out of cheap goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatting is knotting thread by hand into lace; the noun also means cheap rubbish or shoddy goods.

clue.text: One does not approve when this is repeated

definitions.text: One does not approve when this is repeated

parts.words: One does not approve when this is repeated
parts.note: said twice over, this short click of the tongue is the sound a disapproving person makes

explanation.surface: Someone frowns on things said over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: Said twice it is the familiar sound of disapproval; the clue hints at the doubled form.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the clicking exclamation of disapproval, most often doubled as a reproving sound.

clue.text: No time is lost at this

definitions.text: No time is lost at this

parts.words: No time is lost at this
parts.note: put 'at' in front and the phrase means immediately, with no time wasted

explanation.surface: A place where nobody wastes a moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at this' asks you to put 'at' before the answer, giving a phrase meaning immediately.
explanation.definitionFit: Preceded by 'at', the word gives an idiom meaning immediately, without delay.

clue.text: Desk, one found in dilapidated rectories

indicators.note: found in means the numeral for one is placed inside the rearranged letters
dilapidated rectories are falling apart, so the letters of that word are broken up and reassembled

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A writing table turns up in run-down vicarages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dilapidated' rearranges RECTORIES; 'found in' puts I (one) inside those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a writing bureau, a desk with drawers and a fold-down top.

clue.text: Terrorists question the country

parts.note: the IRA, the Irish Republican Army, a paramilitary group often called terrorists in crosswords

explanation.surface: Militants interrogate a nation.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Middle Eastern nation whose capital is Baghdad.

clue.text: Roman poet did nothing with six old pence

parts.note: O is the figure zero, nothing
VI is the Roman numeral for six
D was the abbreviation for pence in Britain's pre-decimal money

explanation.surface: An ancient poet spent nothing but a few coins.
explanation.walkthrough: D, from the Latin denarius, stood for a penny in Britain's old pounds-shillings-pence money.
explanation.definitionFit: He wrote the Metamorphoses in Augustan Rome.

clue.text: Formal protest about gift

parts.note: re is a Latin-derived word meaning about or concerning
a presentation is a formal giving of a gift

explanation.surface: Someone objects officially to a present.
explanation.definitionFit: Representations are formal statements of complaint or argument made to an authority.
